claims.text: Premelting in high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles is governed by the interplay between atomic-scale compositional disorder and surface segregation.
Surface segregation facilitates early surface-atom diffusion that catalyzes premelting.
The initial nanoparticles have a nominally random distribution of multiple elements.
The initial nanoparticles have minimal pre-existing phase segregation.
Local compositional fluctuations at the nanoparticle surface promote selective segregation of lower-melting elements.
At elevated temperatures, regions of the nanoparticle surface become enriched in elements with lower melting points.
Enrichment of surface regions in lower-melting elements enhances surface-atom mobility.
Localized surface premelting propagates into broader melting.
Localized surface premelting reduces the overall melting temperature relative to a well-mixed nanoparticle baseline.
Nanoparticles with greater surface compositional heterogeneity will have a lower onset temperature for observable surface premelting than compositionally uniform nanoparticles.
Nanoparticles with greater surface compositional heterogeneity will have a lower overall melting point than compositionally uniform nanoparticles.
Nanoparticles with minimized surface segregation should exhibit a higher premelting-onset temperature.
Nanoparticles with minimized surface segregation should exhibit a more uniform premelting-onset temperature.
The proposed relationship applies approximately to high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles between 5 and 30 nm.
The relationship applies under heating rates slow enough for surface diffusion to compete with bulk melting.
At extreme particle sizes or rapid heating rates, kinetic effects may cause deviations from the proposed relationship.

A controlled test should compare nanoparticles with intentionally induced surface-composition gradients against nanoparticles with minimized surface segregation under identical heating and environmental conditions.
Failure of the surface-segregated particles to show statistically significant decreases in both premelting onset and overall melting point relative to controls would falsify the hypothesis.
